content: Pemphigoid refers to a group of rare autoimmune diseases characterized by blistering of the skin. As the name suggests, pemphigoid shares similarities with pemphigus; however, unlike pemphigus, pemphigoid does not involve acantholysis, which is the loss of connections between skin cells. Pemphigoid is less common than pemphigus and occurs slightly more frequently in women than in men. It is predominantly observed in individuals over the age of 60, with a lower incidence in younger populations. Classification There are three main types of pemphigoid: 1. Gestational pemphigoid (Pemphigoid gestationis, PG): Previously referred to as herpes gestationis, this form occurs during pregnancy, typically during the second or third trimester, and may also develop immediately after pregnancy. 2. Bullous pemphigoid (BP): This is the most common form and primarily affects older adults, particularly those over the age of 60. 3. Mucous membrane pemphigoid (Cicatricial pemphigoid, CP): This form predominantly involves mucous membranes and is also more common in individuals over 60 years of age. These conditions are classified as connective tissue autoimmune skin diseases. Bullous pemphigoid and cicatricial pemphigoid are most frequently observed in older adults, while gestational pemphigoid is specifically associated with pregnancy.
